notes.meaning: God gave Moses instructions for when an Israelite made a voluntary promise to dedicate a person to the Lord. Because God strictly forbade human sacrifice, vowed persons were not killed; instead, their value was paid in silver to support the sanctuary. Setting a clear price allowed believers to fulfill their religious promises in an orderly and practical way.

An adult male in the prime working years from twenty to sixty was valued at fifty silver pieces, while a woman of the same age was set at thirty pieces. These amounts reflected the general economic value of physical labor in ancient times, not a difference in human worth before God. The money given went directly into the sanctuary treasury.

For young people from five to twenty years of age, the set rate was twenty silver pieces for a male and ten for a female. Parents often made vows dedicating their growing children to God out of gratitude or in answer to prayer. The lower amount reflected the lesser earning power of a youth compared to a full-grown adult.

A child between one month and five years of age had a set value of five silver pieces for a boy and three for a girl. Children under one month old were not given a price because of high infant mortality and early dedication laws. This provision allowed parents to dedicate infants to the Lord while redeeming them with a small payment.

A person sixty years old or older was valued at fifteen silver pieces for a man and ten for a woman. As people grew elderly and passed their peak working years, the required amount was reduced. The difference between men and women also became smaller because their daily labor in the household was more equal in old age.

If someone made a vow but was too poor to pay the standard rate, the priest determined a reduced price that the person could actually afford. God ensured that poverty never prevented anyone from making a heartfelt dedication to Him. The priest looked with mercy on the family's needs so the vow would not ruin them financially.

When an animal suitable for altar sacrifice was vowed to God, it immediately became holy and could not be replaced. The worshiper was forbidden from swapping a better animal for a worse one, or even a worse one for a better one. If an exchange was attempted, both animals became the permanent property of the sanctuary.

An unclean animal that could not be sacrificed on the altar had to be brought before the priest for appraisal. The priest set a fair market price so the animal could be sold for the upkeep of the sanctuary. If the owner wanted to buy it back for himself, he had to pay the assessed price plus an extra twenty percent penalty to discourage careless vows.

When an owner dedicated his house to the Lord, the priest inspected the building and established its value. The house could then be sold to provide money for the tabernacle. If the original owner wished to redeem the house and keep living in it, he was required to add one-fifth to the priest's price.

An Israelite could dedicate a portion of his inherited family land to the sanctuary. The price was not based on soil quality, but on the amount of barley seed needed to plant it, set at fifty silver pieces per large measure of seed. Dedicating only a portion ensured that the family still had enough land left to make a living.

If a field was dedicated right at the start of the fifty-year Jubilee cycle, the price stood at the full valuation. If it was dedicated years later, the priest reduced the price based on how many harvest seasons remained until the next Jubilee. This fair sliding scale matched the true crop value of the land over time.

The man who dedicated his inherited land had the legal right to buy it back at any time. To do so, he had to pay the assessed price along with an extra fifth of its value. Once this full payment was made, the field returned to his family's regular possession.

If the owner refused to buy back the vowed field, or if the sanctuary sold it to someone else, the original owner permanently lost his right of redemption. When the Year of Jubilee arrived, the field did not return to his family line. Instead, it became permanently dedicated to the Lord as the lasting property of the priests.

When someone vowed a field that he had purchased rather than inherited, the priest calculated its value only up to the next Jubilee year. The worshiper paid that amount at once to the sanctuary as a holy gift. At the Jubilee, the land returned to its original hereditary owner according to the general law of property.

Every valuation and payment had to use the official standard weight kept at the sanctuary, which was twenty small units per shekel. Having a single standard prevented dishonest scales and kept all transactions fair and accurate. God demanded total integrity in everything related to holy offerings.

No one could dedicate a firstborn farm animal by a voluntary vow because all firstborn animals already belonged to the Lord by law. Clean firstborn animals like cattle or sheep had to be sacrificed. Unclean firstborn animals, however, could be bought back for their assessed value plus a fifth, or sold by the priests for the sanctuary's benefit.

A special class of vows involved things completely devoted to the Lord under an irreversible ban. Whether it was a person, an animal, or inherited land, anything devoted in this absolute way was declared most holy. It could never be bought back or sold to another person.

Any person placed under the solemn ban of destruction could never be ransomed with money. That person had to be put to death under lawful divine judgment, as was done with idolatrous nations like the Canaanites and Amalekites. This law was not about human sacrifice, but about executing God's legal judgment upon wicked rebels.

One tenth of all grain, seed, and orchard fruit belonged directly to the Lord and was holy to Him. This agricultural tithe served to support the priests and Levites who held no tribal land of their own. If a farmer wanted to keep his grain or fruit, he had to pay its value in money plus an extra twenty percent.

Every tenth animal from cattle or sheep that passed under the shepherd's counting rod belonged to God. The owner was forbidden from sorting out the good animals from the bad or trying to swap them. If an owner attempted to switch any animal, both the original and its substitute became holy to God and neither could be bought back.

The book of Leviticus closes by declaring that these laws came directly from the Lord through Moses for all Israel at Mount Sinai. They provided a complete standard of holy living, worship, and faithful stewardship for God's covenant people. Believers were called to honor their promises and give God first place in all of life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this chapter as an appendix on voluntary gifts that was placed at the end of Leviticus after the formal covenant warnings in chapter 26.
